source.title: Seeing Through Words, Speaking Through Pixels: Deep Representational Alignment Between Vision and Language Models
source.authors: Zoe Wanying He; Sean Trott; Meenakshi Khosla

record.tranche_reason: Measures vision–language representational alignment using linear predictivity and CKA, and tests how it changes under input manipulations and metric choice. It does not reproduce the original scale/performance measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports layer-wise increases with network depth, but depth is not model scale or capability. It also compares vision backbones and reports that objective and data affect alignment; these comparisons do not establish a systematic increase with model size or performance. Rows below focus on input and metric dependence and the reported backbone comparisons. Prior-study results in the introduction are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Measures alignment between unimodal vision and language models on paired image–caption data with ridge linear predictivity and CKA. It varies inputs, aggregation, metric, dataset and vision backbone. It never relates alignment to measured model capability, so the scale/capability parts of V1 and V2 are touched only through two data-scale backbone contrasts.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that unimodal vision and language models converge on a shared semantic code. It peaks in mid-to-late layers, is robust to appearance-only changes but drops under semantic edits, mirrors human preferences, and strengthens with exemplar aggregation. They also caveat that representational similarity is descriptive and does not show functional interchangeability.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ridge-based linear predictivity and CKA to study cross-modal alignment, not the original source’s scale/performance comparison. It also manipulates images and captions and tests preference and embedding aggregation.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment changes with semantic image/caption content, mapping direction, metric, dataset, backbone training objective/data, and whether aggregation uses matched or shuffled image-caption pairs. Grayscale effects differ between the main models and additional LLM-family analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-modal alignment is low in early layers and rises through mid-to-late layers of both models. Language-to-vision predictivity is higher than vision-to-language, and the pattern replicates across datasets and LLM families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision–language representational alignment emerges with network depth and is asymmetric across mapping directions.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed ViT-B/16 size and ImageNet-1k data, AugReg aligned better with LLMs than DINO or DeiT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The vision model's training objective changes cross-modal alignment independently of size and data.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (2025)
record.problems: The backbone comparison does not cleanly disentangle objective and data effects and does not provide a systematic capability scaling test. Several alignment scores are available only in figures. The study uses one sampled set of 1,000 items for its main datasets, synthetic Stable Diffusion images and Gemini-generated paraphrases, and reports representational similarity rather than causal interchangeability. The authors note that the examined metrics are only a subset of possible alignment measures.

untested.parts: No test of alignment against model size or measured capability. Vision-backbone sizes (B vs L) and multiple LLM sizes are used but no size trend is reported.
No test of whether alignment rises as vision and language models both improve; only two data-scale backbone contrasts.
Linear maps are fitted, but the authors say the work shows no functional interchangeability. There is no stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
Mutual k-NN and its neighbour count are not tested. Absolute alignment levels under CKA vs linear predictivity are not compared numerically. No out-of-distribution inputs beyond Flickr8k.
Absolute alignment levels and any plateau with model scale are not reported. Shared-data or shared-objective explanations are not tested.

missing.what: Main-text layer-wise alignment result and its directional asymmetry (no row; only the Flickr8k replication is recorded)
Aggregation of manipulated (nouns-only, scrambled) caption embeddings still raises alignment
Aggregation effects on Flickr8k and in the extra LLM families: alignment rises and plateaus
missing.locator: Appendix D Figure 11; Appendix E Figure 12D

missing.what: Absolute alignment levels: no numeric linear-predictivity or CKA scores in text, so completeness of convergence cannot be read
Multiple BLOOM/OpenLLaMA and ViT sizes were used, but no alignment-vs-size comparison is reported in text

record.verdict_notes: r1-r3 were moved from V1-only to V1/V2 (r2, r3) and none (r1): they are vision-to-LLM comparisons that vary data and objective, and capability is never measured. V6 states were changed from partial to observed where alignment significantly weakened, since V6 says 'weakens or vanishes'. Sign convention: positive t means lower alignment after manipulation, so r7's negative significant t is an increase. The CKA replication reproduces the direction of the input effects, so the study gives no evidence that the effects vanish under another metric, except the thing-only drop (r29). The text says 'seven vision–language model pairs' in §3.3 but uses n=8 throughout (t(7)); minor inconsistency.

versions.untested_parts: Backbone comparisons vary size, objective, and data but do not systematically relate model size or capability to alignment across independently trained models.
The study measures cross-modal alignment, but does not test whether alignment increases as both vision and language models improve in capability.
No comparison of independently initialized seeds of the same architecture.
No test of stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data as an interchangeability claim.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features or circuits.
Tests image and caption manipulations, a shuffled-pair baseline, and CKA as an alternative metric; does not test neighbourhood-count settings or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not establish that alignment is incomplete or plateaus as models scale, or test whether shared training data/objectives explain alignment instead of a common semantic structure.

rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment with language models across vision backbones differing in objective, data, and size, in the caption-embedding averaging analysis.

conditions.value: AugReg, DINO, DINOv2, DeiT; seven backbones overall

rows.measure: Linear predictivity alignment; directional differences across backbones were described, but individual scores are figure-only.
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Objective and data differences affected alignment; AugReg was higher than DINO and DeiT when model size and data were held constant (ViT-B/16, ImageNet-1k).
rows.note: The text says that the interaction of objective and data could not be cleanly disentangled. This is not a controlled size–capability scaling result.
rows.check: Compares objectives (AugReg vs DINO vs DeiT) at fixed size and data, not models getting larger or better. It does not measure what V1 or V2 names; moved to fits_no_version.

rows.value: DINOv2-LVD142m aligned more strongly; numeric score not stated.
rows.note: This compares a dataset change, not a controlled increase in model size or capability.
